name: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
title: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
answer: Board advisory and fiduciary risk covers how directors oversee an organization's use of AI, including generative tools, automated decisions, and third-party models. It addresses the duty of care and duty of loyalty as they apply to AI adoption, vendor selection, and internal deployment. The work focuses on identifying where AI can create financial, reputational, legal, or operational harm that a board should reasonably anticipate. It also includes advising boards on the questions to ask management about AI governance, testing, and incident response.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This practice runs on board meeting materials, risk registers, and AI use case inventories that map each system to its owner, data sources, and decision rights. It relies on compliance monitoring feeds, regulatory trackers, and internal audit reports that flag changes in AI law and enforcement. Many teams use secure document repositories to maintain board packs, minutes, and evidence of oversight. The site's 210 compliance and regulation pages and 6823 state AI bills provide a reference base for tracking obligations that boards must consider.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by first inventorying where AI is used or planned across the business, then mapping each use to the fiduciary duties of care, loyalty, and oversight. Advisors review model documentation, training data provenance, and human review procedures to assess whether the board has enough information to approve or monitor a system. They prepare board briefings that translate technical risk into business and legal exposure, and they test whether management's AI policies align with the board's risk appetite. Regular horizon scanning for new lawsuits, enforcement actions, and regulatory guidance keeps the board's questions current.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance center on who is accountable when an AI system causes harm, and whether the board can show it acted with due care. Boards face exposure if they approve high-risk AI without understanding its limits, or if they fail to ask about data provenance, bias testing, or third-party indemnities. Documentation matters: minutes, risk assessments, and vendor contracts create the record that regulators and plaintiffs will review. The site's tracking of 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, shows the concrete litigation risk that boards must weigh, though no page here is legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Board advisory in this area is moving toward explicit AI oversight duties, with regulators and investors expecting directors to demonstrate AI literacy and challenge management on model risk. Fiduciary standards will likely require boards to document why a particular AI use is in the company's best interest, including alternatives considered and harms assessed. Expect more board-level AI committees, mandatory AI risk disclosures, and closer scrutiny of supply chain and training data provenance. The practice will shift from reactive legal review to continuous fiduciary monitoring as AI becomes embedded in core operations.
